Predictions from a panel instrumental-variables fit

Source: R/predict-extra.R
predict.paniv.Rd

Linear predictions from a paniv() fit. For model = "pooling", "random" and "hausmantaylor" the prediction is the linear index x'b (with the intercept), the conditional mean given the regressors that does not involve the individual effect; this is what predict() returns for AER::ivreg() and plm::plm() fits of these models. For model = "within" the estimated individual effects a_i = mean_t(y_it - x_it'b) are added (and, for effect = "twoways", the time effects, from the two-way decomposition of y - x'b), as in predict.panglm().

Usage

# S3 method for class 'paniv'
predict(object, newdata = NULL, allow.new.levels = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

object

a "paniv" fit

newdata

optional data frame

allow.new.levels

for within fits, if TRUE an individual (or time period) of newdata that is not in the fit gets an effect of zero, so that its prediction is the linear index x'b; if FALSE (default) it is an error

...

unused

Value

a numeric vector of predictions, one per row of newdata (NA where a regressor is missing)

Details

Without newdata the in-sample fitted values are returned in the row order of the fitting data (with NA for the rows dropped by na.action). With newdata, the regressors of the first part of the formula are evaluated on newdata; factor regressors must carry the levels used in the fit. For within fits newdata must contain the panel index columns.

Validation

Numerical accuracy is checked in the package tests and in the validation suite; see the validation article on the package website.

See also

Other paniv methods: summary.paniv(), vcov.paniv()

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(id = rep(1:50, each = 4), t = rep(1:4, 50))
d$z <- rnorm(200); d$u <- rnorm(200)
d$x <- d$z + d$u + rnorm(200)
d$y <- 1 + d$x + d$u + rep(rnorm(50), each = 4) + rnorm(200)
fit <- paniv(y ~ x | z, data = d, index = c("id", "t"), model = "within")
head(predict(fit))
#> [1]  2.1897524  5.4910216  1.3851551  2.2080306 -0.3994349  3.7668555
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(id = 1:2, t = 5, x = 0))
#> [1] 1.217343 2.290716
